en: When Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva offered the Buddha the dhāraṇī named Usuta—
translated here as "Extinction of Lust and Rejection of Arrogance"—
the Buddha commanded Ānanda to widely proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings who will suffer in the future. At that time...
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva first spoke these verses:
"Of all classes of sentient beings, Those who have fallen and drowned in the realm of lustful demons— None are able to awaken them; Only I can rescue and deliver them."
Having forever severed the root of birth and death, one universally abides in the bliss of quiescence.
Then he spoke the dhāraṇī, saying:

*ku li ku li te na u cu u cu te na du hu du hu te na ku ṭa ku ṭa te na ja mi du ja mi du te na ku ṭa hu ku ṭa hu te na u shu u shu te na ya mi ja ya mi ja te na du hu ṭa ku ṭa ta sarva svāhā.* Recite this mantra three times.
Tie seven knots made of hempen thread and fasten them to the feet;
this mantra can cause those who have lost their minds to regain right mindfulness.
Extinguish the fire of lustful desire and sever the fetters of pride.
When the impurities of the three poisons are exhausted, one naturally becomes cool and serene.
If there is spirit, [it will manifest].
They sink beneath the heavy abyss of ignorance;
long submerged in birth and death, they find no way of escape.
Alas! How deeply pitiable this is.
If a person’s mind attains awakening and feels extreme self-loathing toward defilement,
[they realize] that this is the sphere of activity of ordinary, foolish, base beings— gods, ghosts, and animals—
and is not suitable for the holy life (brahmacarya).
This is not what the noble ones desire.
Only such a person as this may receive and uphold this dhāraṇī.
Do not transmit it to those who feign worldly piety, harbor doubt and slander, or possess little faith.
Even if there is no immediate efficacy while maintaining the practice, one will eventually turn back from decline; however,
for those who recite with utmost sincerity, the fire of desire gradually subsides,
the fetters are extinguished, and the mind attains liberation.
Once the mind is liberated, one attains the fruit of the Path.
This is the true and non-deceptive efficacy of supernatural power.
Those who practice this Dharma must abstain from alcohol, the five pungent roots, and meat.
For a man, it takes exactly eighty-one days (nine times nine);
for a woman, it takes exactly forty-nine days (seven times seven).
During the six periods of day and night, one should diligently recite with a focused mind.
Burn aloeswood and white sandalwood incense and scatter flowers as offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
do so three times during the day and three times at night, being careful not to neglect or forget this.
During the remaining time before the days [of the retreat] have expired,
one should dwell alone in a mountain cave, a vihāra,
or— if in a village— a pure chamber situated far from people in all four directions.
One should give rise to deep joy and spontaneously feel fortunate, thinking:
"Now that I have encountered the spiritual power of the Great Sage,
this body shall surely attain the state of a Buddha's body."
Without fear of sinking or drowning,
one thus purifies the mind, maintaining faith and orientation in every thought-moment;
one abandons all evil deeds, turns away from miscellaneous talk and divisive speech.
He does not dwell upon fame or profit.
Once the prescribed number of days is completed, his mind is definitively liberated;
it becomes serene, and he is no longer subject to desire or pride.
